Tom is based in the UK and when he's not writing about TV shows, he's watching them. He's also an avid horror fiction writer, gamer, and has a Dungeons and Dragons habit that he tries (and fails) to keep in check.

There's no shortage of original sci-fi TV shows on Prime Video. The streaming service has made ambitious speculative storytelling a part of its identity, offering everything from sprawling space-operas like The Expanse to disturbing glimpses into dystopian cyberpunk futures like The Peripheral. The levels of both variety and quality make Prime Video an ideal destination for anyone seeking a new sci-fi series to get lost in regardless of the specific subgenre.

However, many of the best Prime Video sci-fi shows are also commitments. Series like The Expanse and The Boys are sprawling, multi-season sagas that even dedicated bingewatchers would struggle to finish over a single weekend. Embarking on their journies can feel like an undertaking before the first episode has even started. That's precisely why Tales from the Loop is such a breath of fresh air. It offers the imagination and emotional ambition of any of the greatest Prime sci-fi series, but in a far more manageable package.

Inspired by Simon Stålenhag's paintings, Tales from the Loop follows a community living above an underground facility where extraordinary scientific discoveries reshape ordinary lives. Its eight interconnected episodes explore everything from altered timelines to parallel dimensions, all the while keeping the focus on the people affected rather than the grand concepts. The result is an amazing collection of sci-fi stories that now serves as one of Prime Video's most bingeable creations. Taking less than eight hours to finish, Tales from the Loop offers a compact weekend viewing experience without sacrificing complexity or impact.
It’s Hard Not To Binge Tales From The Loop

blocks.c: Gaddis standing in front of a floating tractor in Tales From the Loop

blocks.x: There are plenty of bingeable sci-fi shows out there, especially on Prime Video, but Tales from the Loop stands out because its appeal has little to do with relentless cliffhangers. It’s patient, often melancholy viewing, with each story being self-contained. The “next episode” button becomes impossible to ignore not because of unresolved questions, but from growing attached to the occupants of the town and gradually understanding how their seemingly separate experiences fit together.

The anthology structure gives each Tales from the Loop episode its own central characters and uniquely weird sci-fi premise, while its compact, miniseries-length run allows those stories to quickly build into something larger. Supporting figures in one episode become protagonists of their own a few episodes later, and seemingly inconsequential relationships, interactions, and moments take on new significance. Watching episodes of Tales from the Loop back-to-back makes those connections especially rewarding.

Best of all, with eight episodes running roughly an hour apiece, the complete experience can be devoured across a weekend. Tales from the Loop perfectly demonstrates how small-screen sci-fi can flourish on streaming: individual stories have room to breathe, while immediate access to the next installment lets their emotional connections remain fresh. A weekend offers more than enough time to appreciate both the individual chapters and the larger story of one of the best sci-fi TV shows Prime Video has to offer.
Tales From The Loop Deserves Much More Recognition

blocks.c: A boy with a robot in Tales from the Loop

blocks.x: Tales from the Loop may be one of the best sci-fi shows on Prime Video, but it’s also incredibly underrated. It deserves a far more prominent place in discussions about the best modern small-screen science fiction. Not just because it’s so bingeable, either. The way it treats impossible events as intimate experiences feels truly unique. The science-fiction trappings may be fantastical and jaw-dropping, but the feelings and troubles of the characters encountering them remain recognizable: loneliness, jealousy, grief, and the desire to hold onto people who cannot stay are much more central than any sci-fi concept.

The retro-futuristic world and aesthetic of Tales from the Loop is equally distinctive. Enormous machines and abandoned technology occupy quiet landscapes, making the extraordinary seem embedded in everyday life. The show’s measured pacing then allows viewers to absorb themselves in these surroundings and take in how they’re the product of the uneasy relationship between scientific possibility and human vulnerability.

Where many modern sci-fi shows build momentum through escalating threats or increasingly elaborate mythology, Tales from the Loop finds lasting power in smaller consequences. Its mysteries don’t demand technical explanations, as it’s their emotional meaning and symbolic significance that carries the stories. It’s an exceptional level of restraint for a sci-fi show, and this is where the true genius of Tales from the Loop can be found. Few series offer such a coherent combination of speculative imagination, visual beauty, and emotional depth within such a digestible runtime.
Andrew Stanton, Dearbhla Walsh, Jodie Foster, So Yong Kim, Charlie McDowell, Ti West
